subject: Accounting & Auditing
title: Paper I - Cost & Managerial Accounting (50 Marks)

segments.text: This paper asks how cost information is built, and then how it is used for planning and decisions. The logical order: classify costs and their elements, accumulate them through job or process costing, turn plans into budgets, use contribution and break-even thinking for short-term decisions, and finally compare planned against actual performance through standard costing and variances. Keep the decision purpose in view throughout: the same cost figure can matter for different reasons depending on what question is being asked.

blocks.text: A. Three Accounting Lenses on the Same Business

segments.text: Financial, cost, and management accounting are not three separate subjects; they are three questions asked of the same underlying data.

items.text: Financial accounting reports overall performance and position to broad external users, following prescribed formats.
Cost accounting measures and assigns cost to products, jobs, or services, so that a per-unit or per-job cost figure can be produced.
Management accounting uses both financial and non-financial information to help managers plan, decide, and control, often with no prescribed format at all.

segments.text: Example: a cost sheet built by cost accounting shows the unit manufacturing cost of a product; management accounting then uses that same figure to decide pricing or which product mix to emphasize. A useful way to compare the three is along purpose, users, time orientation, level of detail, and degree of external regulation.

blocks.text: B. Cost Concepts, Elements and Classification

segments.text: A cost is simply a resource sacrifice measured for a stated purpose, and the same cost can honestly be described several different ways depending on why it is being classified.

items.text: By element: direct material (traceable raw material), direct labour (traceable wages), and manufacturing overhead (everything else needed to run the factory that cannot be economically traced to a single unit).
By behaviour: fixed (does not change with activity within a relevant range, such as factory rent) versus variable (changes roughly in proportion to activity, such as material used per unit).
By traceability: direct (traced to one cost object) versus indirect (shared across several cost objects and assigned on some basis).
By financial reporting role: product cost (attached to the unit and expensed only when sold) versus period cost (expensed in the period incurred, regardless of sales).
By decision relevance: controllable versus uncontrollable, and relevant versus irrelevant to a specific decision (see Section F).

segments.text: Example: factory rent is typically indirect and fixed within a relevant range, while material used specifically in one product is typically direct and variable. The exam skill is not reciting definitions but correctly classifying a mixed list of real costs, because the same rent figure could be called fixed in one question and irrelevant in another, depending on what is being asked.

blocks.text: C. Material, Labour and Factory Overhead

segments.text: These are the three manufacturing cost elements in more depth.

items.text: Material: accounting tracks purchase, storage, issue, and use of raw material. Control aims to avoid shortages, excess stock, waste, and loss while keeping production running, using inventory records, reorder decisions, and a chosen valuation or issue method. If production requires 100 units of raw material, the stores record should show the authorized issue and the remaining balance, linking physical control to accounting control.

Labour: workers can be paid by time worked (time rate), output produced (piece rate), or an incentive scheme that rewards productivity while sharing the benefit with the worker. Example: Rs 500 per unit times 20 units gives a piece-rate gross amount of Rs 10,000, before other payroll effects. Direct labour is assigned to the specific job or process it worked on; indirect labour, such as a supervisor’s wage, is treated as overhead.

Factory overhead (FOH): includes manufacturing costs that cannot be economically traced directly to one job or unit, such as indirect material, indirect labour, and factory utilities. Because it cannot be traced directly, it must be collected and then assigned to production using a rational base, often through a predetermined overhead rate calculated as budgeted overhead divided by budgeted activity. Example: budgeted FOH of Rs 1,200,000 over 60,000 budgeted labour hours gives a predetermined rate of Rs 20 per labour hour. Applying this rate to actual hours worked, and comparing it to actual overhead incurred, produces over-absorption or under-absorption of overhead.

segments.text: Overhead often has to be shared across several departments before it can be applied to production, and this happens in two stages.

items.text: Allocation: a whole cost is charged directly to one department, because it clearly belongs there.

Apportionment: a common cost is divided among several departments on a reasonable basis. Example: canteen cost may be apportioned by number of employees in each department; power cost may be apportioned by machine hours or meter readings.

Reapportionment: after this primary distribution, service-department costs (canteen, maintenance, stores) are moved on to the production departments they actually support, using methods such as repeated distribution or algebraic methods when departments provide services to each other reciprocally.

segments.text: The underlying logic is always the same: costs should end up resting on the production departments that ultimately caused them, even when they were first recorded against a department that does not itself make anything.

blocks.text: E. Job-Order Costing and Process Costing

segments.text: Both are methods for accumulating production cost, and the first decision is which one fits the business: is output made as distinguishable, separately identifiable jobs, or as a continuous flow of similar units?

items.text: Job-order costing accumulates cost for a specific job, batch, or customer order. A job cost sheet collects direct material, direct labour, and applied overhead for that one job. Example: a custom furniture order’s manufacturing cost is built from the wood used, the carpenter’s hours, and the overhead assigned to that job.

Process costing is used when many similar units flow through continuous stages, such as a chemical plant passing material through a Mixing department and then a Finishing department. Costs are accumulated by process or department and averaged over output. A cost of production report is the working document that explains the physical flow of units, equivalent production where partially completed units exist, cost per equivalent unit, and how total cost is assigned between units finished and units still in process.

segments.text: In both methods, keep physical units and cost flows as two separate tracking exercises, especially wherever work-in-process is involved, because confusing the two is the most common source of errors.

A budget is a quantified plan for a future period, converting objectives into expected sales, production, resource, cash, and financial outcomes. Budgets should be read as a linked system, not as separate isolated formats.

items.text: Sales budget: estimates units and revenue to be sold, and it is the starting point that drives everything else.

Production budget: estimates units to produce, following the relation Production equals Sales plus Desired Ending Finished Goods minus Opening Finished Goods. Example: expected sales 10,000, desired ending inventory 1,500, opening inventory 1,000, gives a production requirement of 10,500 units. Because opening inventory for one month is the previous month’s closing inventory, this formula links one period to the next.

Cash budget: forecasts cash receipts, payments, financing needs, and ending cash. A profitable company can still face a cash shortage if collections from customers arrive after its own payments are due. Example: opening cash 100, receipts 500, payments 550, gives an ending balance of 50 before any financing is arranged. Non-cash expenses like depreciation are excluded from a cash budget, since they involve no cash movement.

Flexible, zero-based, and master budgets: a flexible budget adjusts allowed costs and revenues to the actual activity level actually achieved, which is fairer than a static budget when comparing performance. Example: comparing actual cost at 12,000 units against a static budget built for 10,000 units is misleading; a flexible budget restates the expected cost for 12,000 units before comparing. Zero-based budgeting requires every activity to be justified from a zero base each period rather than simply rolling forward last year’s numbers plus an increase. The master budget is the full integrated set of operating and financial budgets, built up from the sales budget through to a budgeted income statement and balance sheet.

segments.text: When actual results are later compared with any budget, the key analytical skill is separating a difference caused by a different activity level from one caused by price, efficiency, or a planning assumption that turned out to be wrong — a budget is only useful when the reason behind a variance can be explained, not merely reported.

blocks.text: G. Marginal (Variable) Costing versus Absorption Costing

segments.text: The two methods differ in exactly one respect: how fixed manufacturing overhead is treated.

items.text: Variable (marginal) costing treats fixed manufacturing overhead as a period cost, expensed in full in the period it is incurred, regardless of how much was sold.
Absorption costing includes fixed manufacturing overhead inside product cost, so a portion of it sits in inventory value whenever some units produced are not yet sold.

segments.text: This single difference means the two methods can report different profit figures whenever production and sales volumes differ within a period. Example: if production exceeds sales, some units remain in closing inventory, and under absorption costing a slice of fixed overhead sits inside that inventory value rather than hitting the income statement, so absorption-costing profit is typically higher than variable-costing profit in that period. When production equals sales, the two methods give the same profit, because no fixed overhead is left behind in inventory. Being able to reconcile the profit figures between the two methods (the difference equals the fixed overhead in the change in inventory) is a core exam skill.

blocks.text: H. Contribution, Cost-Volume-Profit Analysis and Break-Even

segments.text: Contribution is the foundation for almost every short-term decision technique in this paper: Contribution per unit equals Selling price minus Variable cost per unit. Contribution first covers fixed cost; whatever is left over after that becomes profit. Example: selling price 100, variable cost 60, gives a contribution of 40 per unit. The contribution margin ratio, contribution divided by sales, expresses this as a percentage.

Cost-volume-profit (CVP) analysis studies how volume, price, variable cost, and fixed cost interact to determine profit, and break-even point is its simplest application: the activity level at which total contribution exactly equals fixed cost, so profit is exactly zero.

items.text: Break-even units equal Fixed Cost divided by Contribution per unit.
Break-even sales value equals Fixed Cost divided by Contribution margin ratio.

segments.text: Example: fixed cost 200,000, contribution 40 per unit, gives a break-even point of 5,000 units. The same logic extends naturally to target-profit questions (treat the target profit as an addition to fixed cost in the formula) and margin-of-safety questions (how far actual or budgeted sales exceed the break-even point, which measures how much sales can fall before a loss occurs).

Decision-making requires incremental thinking, not blindly reading off full accounting cost. Relevant costs are future costs and revenues that actually differ between the alternatives being compared; sunk costs, already incurred in the past, do not change with today’s decision and should be ignored no matter how large they were. Example: a machine bought last year for Rs 1,000,000 is a sunk historical cost when deciding today whether to accept a special order; only future avoidable costs and incremental revenues matter to that decision. This logic underlies a family of standard question types at this syllabus level: make-or-buy, accepting a special order, allocating a scarce (limiting) resource across products, deciding whether to discontinue or retain a product line, and equipment-replacement decisions. In each case, the exam technique is the same: list only the costs and revenues that change between the alternatives, ignore sunk costs and costs common to all alternatives, and compare the incremental result.

blocks.text: J. Standard Costing and Variance Analysis

segments.text: A standard is a planned benchmark for quantity or price, set in advance of production. A variance is simply the difference between standard (expected) and actual performance, and its purpose is to prompt management to investigate why results differed from the plan — a variance is a starting point for asking why, not an end in itself.
The syllabus groups variances into material, labour, and factory-overhead variances, and each of these can usually be split into two underlying causes:

items.text: A price or rate effect: did we pay a different price (for material) or rate (for labour) than planned?
A quantity or efficiency effect: did we use a different quantity of material, or take a different amount of time, than planned?

segments.text: Example: if material was budgeted to cost Rs 10 per kilogram but actually cost Rs 11 per kilogram, that difference contributes to an unfavourable material price variance, separate from any variance caused by using more or less material than the standard allowed for the output actually achieved. The most reliable way to learn the formulas is to first be able to state, in plain words, what each variance is actually asking, and only then attach the formula to that question.

Paper I (Cost & Managerial Accounting) key takeaways: financial, cost, and management accounting are three different questions asked of the same data, not three unrelated subjects. The same cost can be validly classified several different ways depending on the purpose of the question. Overhead has to be allocated, apportioned, and then reapportioned before it reaches production departments. Job costing suits distinguishable jobs; process costing suits a continuous flow of similar units. Budgets form one linked system driven by the sales forecast. Absorption and variable costing differ only in the treatment of fixed manufacturing overhead, and this alone can explain a profit difference between them. Contribution is the foundation of break-even and CVP analysis. Only future, incremental costs and revenues are relevant to a decision; sunk costs are never relevant. Every variance decomposes into a price/rate effect and a quantity/efficiency effect, and the formula matters less than being able to state what question the variance is actually answering.
